blocks.text: If it is asked how an olive branch with green leaves could have lasted so long under the waters, I shall have two things to answer. First, although in Jerome's version Noah's dove is read to have carried in her mouth a branch with green leaves, yet in the Hebrew we read only that she had in her mouth עלה זית טרף, an olive leaf plucked off. Second, the ancients report that certain species not only of the olive but of other trees too live and stay green under water. Theophrastus, Hist. Plant. book 4, chapter 8: Ἐν δὲ τῇ θαλάττῃ ἐρυθρᾷ δενδρά τινα φύεται· καὶ καλοῦσιν αὐτὰ δάφνην, καὶ ἐλαίαν. Ἔστι δὲ ἡ μὲν δάφνη ὅμοια τῇ ἀρίᾳ, ἡ δὲ ἐλαία τῷ φύλλῳ· καρπὸν δὲ ἔχει ἡ ἐλαία παραπλήσιον δὲ ταῖς ἐλαίαις [En de tē thalattē erythra dendra tina phyetai; kai kalousin auta daphnēn, kai elaian. Esti de hē men daphnē homoia tē aria, hē de elaia tō phyllō; karpon de echei hē elaia paraplēsion de tais elaiais]. Pliny condenses this in book 13, ch. 25: But in the Red Sea (it is a marvel) woods live, chiefly the laurel and the olive, bearing berries. And Theophrastus again: Ἐν δὲ ταῖς νήσοις ταῖς ὑπὸ τῆς πλυμμυρίδος καταλαμβανομέναις, δένδρα μεγάλα πεφυκέναι ἡλίκα πλάτανοι· συμβαίνειν δὲ ὅθ᾽ ἡ πλημμυρὶς ἐπέλθοι, τὰ μὲν ἄλλα κατακρύπτεσθαι ὅλα, τῶν δὲ μεγίστων ὑπερέχειν τοὺς κλάδους [En de tais nēsois tais hypo tēs plymmyridos katalambanomenais, dendra megala pephykenai hēlika platanoi; symbainein de hoth᾽ hē plēmmyris epelthoi, ta men alla katakryptesthai hola, tōn de megistōn hyperechein tous kladous], etc. ἔχειν δὲ τὰ δένδρα φύλλον μὲν ὅμοιον τῇ δάφνῃ, ἄνθος δὲ τοῖς οἴσοις [echein de ta dendra phyllon men homoion tē daphnē, anthos de tois oisois] (read with Pliny τοῖς ἴοις [tois iois]) καὶ τῷ χρώματι, καὶ τῇ ὀσμῇ, καρπὸν δ᾽ ἡλίκον ἐλαίᾳ, καὶ τοῦτον εὐώδη σφόδρα, καὶ τὰ μὲν φύλλα οὐκ ἀποβάλλειν, τὸ δὲ ἄνθος, καὶ τὸν καρπὸν ἅμα τῷ φθινοπώρῳ γίνεσθαι· τοῦ δὲ ἔαρος ἀποῤῥεῖν [kai tō chrōmati, kai tē osmē, karpon d᾽ hēlikon elaia, kai touton euōdē sphodra, kai ta men phylla ouk apoballein, to de anthos, kai ton karpon hama tō phthinopōrō ginesthai; tou de earos aporrhein]. Pliny rendered this as follows, with the order somewhat changed: In the same region the tide covers woods of islands, although they are taller than plane trees and the tallest poplars. Their leaves are those of the laurel, the flower is that of the violet in scent and colour, the berries are like olives, and they too have a pleasant scent; they grow in autumn, and the leaves never fall. The sea covers the smaller of these entirely; the tops of the largest stand out. Theophrastus adds: Ἀλλὰ δὲ ἐν αὐτῇ τῇ θαλάττῃ πεφυκέναι, ἀείφυλλα μὲν, τὸν δὲ καρπὸν ὅμοιον ἔχειν τοῖς θέρμοις [Alla de en autē tē thalattē pephykenai, aeiphylla men, ton de karpon homoion echein tois thermois]. Hence Pliny: Other trees too have been seen in the deep, etc. in the same sea, always retaining their leaves, their fruit like the lupine. Plutarch too, in the book On the Face in the Orb of the Moon: Τῆς δὲ Γεδρωσίας καὶ Τρωγλοδύτιδος ἡ καθήκει πρὸς τὸν ὠκεανὸν, ἀφόρου διὰ ξηρότητα, καὶ ἀδένδρου παντάπασιν οὔσης, ἐν τῇ παρακειμένῃ καὶ παρακεχυμένῃ [col. 30] θαλάττῃ θαυμαστὰ μεγέθη φυτῶν τρέφεται, καὶ κατὰ βυθοῦ τέθηλεν· ὧν τὰ μὲν ἐλαίας, τὰ δὲ δάφνας, τὰ Ἴσιδος τρίχας καλοῦσιν [Tēs de Gedrōsias kai Trōglodytidos hē kathēkei pros ton ōkeanon, aphorou dia xērotēta, kai adendrou pantapasin ousēs, en tē parakeimenē kai parakechymenē thalattē thaumasta megethē phytōn trephetai, kai kata bythou tethēlen; hōn ta men elaias, ta de daphnas, ta Isidos trichas kalousin]. But that part of the Gedrosian and Troglodytic region which reaches to the ocean, although it is wholly [II, 563] barren through dryness and lacks trees, yet in the neighbouring sea that washes it plants of unusual size grow and sprout from the depths; some of them they call olives, others laurels, others hairs of Isis. I think Plutarch has this from Agatharchides, in whom some things are read, book 5, chapter 53, about olives in the sea and the hairs of Isis, but interpolated by Photius. The tree in the sea like a plane tree, of which Theophrastus and Pliny speak, is called in Arabic قرم [qurm] Karam. Alcamus: القرم نبت كالدلب غلظا وبياضا ينبت في البحر جوف [al-qurm nabt ka-l-dulb ghilaẓan wa-bayāḍan yanbut fī al-baḥr jawf] The alkaram grows like a plane tree, a large and white tree. It comes up in the middle of the sea ^{(1)}. Since it is clear from these passages that true trees live in the sea itself, and among them a tree most like the olive, which therefore not only Pliny but also the inhabitants of those places simply call an olive: why should not an olive, whose leaves never fall (whence the Poet,

have kept its leaves under the waters for several months, or at least some one of them, which was plucked by the dove? All the more so, since it may be gathered that olive leaves long withstand water and rain from the fact that the Ichthyophagi cover their huts with them. Strabo, book 16, speaks of μάνδρας στεγαστὰς ἀπὸ φυλλάδος ἐλαίνης [mandras stegastas apo phyllados elainēs], huts roofed with olive leaf. And Agatharchides, book 5, ch. 17: Οἱ δὲ τὰς τῶν ἐλαιῶν κορυφὰς ἀλλήλαις συνάπτοντες εἶτα χρῶνται σκηνώμασι [Hoi de tas tōn elaiōn koryphas allēlais synaptontes eita chrōntai skēnōmasi]; Others use the tops of olives, joined to one another, as tents. And Diodorus, book 3, p. 109: Ἐλαίαι φύονται πάνυ πολλαὶ περὶ τοὺς τόπους τούτους, τὰ μὲν πρὸς τὴν ῥίζαν ἔχουσαι προσκλυζόμενα τῇ θαλάττη, πυκναὶ δὲ τοῖς φυλλώμασι [Elaiai phyontai pany pollai peri tous topous toutous, ta men pros tēn rhizan echousai prosklyzomena tē thalattē, pyknai de tois phyllōmasi], etc. ταύτας ἀλλήλαις συμπλέκοντες, καὶ συνεχῆ σκιὰν ποιοῦντες, ἰδιαζούσαις σκηναῖς ἐμβιοῦσιν [tautas allēlais symplekontes, kai synechē skian poiountes, idiazousais skēnais embiousin]. Very many olives grow around those places, with their roots immersed in the sea and with very dense foliage. Weaving these together and making a continuous shade, they live in them privately as in tents. For ἐλαίαι [elaiai], that is, olives, our editions wrongly have ἐλάται [elatai], firs, whose leaves are too narrow to make a continuous shade. Diodorus must therefore be corrected from Agatharchides and Strabo.
